title: Why This Wyoming Town Says Its Own Name Wrong on Purpose
description:
Dubois, Wyoming, is spelled like a French name, but the people who live there say "DOO-boys." The story goes that they do it on purpose, to spite the politician from Idaho whose name replaced the one they had chosen. Here is what is known, what is disputed, and what is local legend.

Chapters
0:00 Why do they say it wrong?
0:28 65 miles for a letter
1:05 Tibo

2:11 Four suspects

Facts used: Homesteaders on Horse Creek in the upper Wind River valley wanted a post office; the nearest was about 65 miles away at Fort Washakie, and for about a year settlers packed mail from the fort to Charles Smith's cabin. In 1889, a year before statehood, the application named the office "Tibo," a Shoshone word for "stranger" or "white man" and the Shoshone people's affectionate name for the Welsh Episcopal priest John Roberts, who arrived at Fort Washakie in 1883 and also served the Horse Creek homesteaders. The application was amended in red ink to "Dubois." The post office opened on Aug. 6, 1889, with Charles C. Smith as postmaster; one local account says Smith could not write and Billy (William Lee) Simpson may have filled out the form. Accounts disagree on who chose the name: Fred Dubois himself, Wyoming's congressional delegate Joseph Carey for his friend, postmaster Hewie Youmans, or Simpson, who told a Casper newspaper in 1937 that it was his idea, after a Dubois family he knew in Colorado. Fred Dubois (1851-1930), born in Illinois and a Yale graduate, was a U.S. marshal in Idaho Territory who campaigned to disenfranchise Mormon voters, Idaho's delegate to Congress from 1887 and its senator from 1891; Dubois, Idaho, is also named after him. Historian Leo Graff wrote that he disliked hearing his name said as "boys." The idea that locals say "DOO-boys" to spite him is local legend; another theory is that it is simply how the word was read. One Arapaho name for the town translates as "two boys." Butch Cassidy arrived in the valley in the fall of 1889 and ranched on Horse Creek with Al Hainer (tax records show $27.11 owed for 1890); he was arrested for horse theft in 1892 and imprisoned in 1894. Neversweat was a separate post office about 15 miles away (1895-1897), not an earlier name for Dubois. Dubois was incorporated in 1914; its ZIP code area is larger than Rhode Island. Sources include Cowboy State Daily (2025, 2026), WyoHistory.org, the Wyoming State Library's place-name records, and the University of Colorado Arapaho Language Project.
